title: From Zero to Hero: An Open LLM Ecosystem for Armenian
gist: The COPA team released ArmWeb (a deduplicated, contamination-scanned Armenian news corpus) and ArmSTEM (a verified translated math/science corpus), and used them to continued-pretrain Gemma-4-E4B into arm-gemma-e4b, the first open Armenian LLM published with every training token and hyperparameter public, and the first adapted open Armenian model that outperforms its own base — while their ablations show most prior Armenian language-adaptation fine-tunes actually degrade knowledge capability via catastrophic forgetting.

themes.theme: Headline result and its statistical weight

insights.claim: arm-gemma-e4b, a Gemma-4-E4B model continued-pretrained on Armenian data, is the only open adapted Armenian model the authors are aware of that scores above its own unadapted base model on a six-task Armenian likelihood benchmark suite.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: A concrete, verifiable claim of state-of-the-art for open Armenian LLMs; worth tracking as a template other low-resource-language teams may replicate or challenge.
insights.quote: It is the only open adapted Armenian model we know of that ends above its base.

insights.claim: On the six-task suite, arm-gemma-e4b posts a mean score of 0.50 versus 0.48 for the unadapted Gemma-4-E4B base, versus 0.47 for ArmenianGPT-1.0-3B, 0.44 for HyGPT-10b, and 0.35 for tweety-7b.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Quantifies the new open-source ceiling for Armenian LLM knowledge tasks, a reference point for anyone benchmarking or investing in Armenian-language AI tooling.

insights.claim: The per-model 95% confidence interval half-width on the benchmark mean is about ±0.010, so arm-gemma-e4b's +2.2-point gain over its base model sits well outside the noise band.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Confirms the reported gain is statistically real rather than single-seed noise, strengthening confidence in the headline claim.

themes.theme: The forgetting arc: why most language-adaptation fine-tunes backfire

insights.claim: Continued pretraining on news-only Armenian text at a high learning rate (1e-4) destroys 21 points of reading comprehension (Belebele score falls from 0.619 to 0.407), with the damage complete by mid-training so checkpoint selection cannot rescue it.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Demonstrates catastrophic forgetting can be severe and irreversible mid-run for naive language-adaptation recipes, a real risk for anyone continued-pretraining a base model on a new language without careful ablation.

insights.claim: Swapping just 6 points of the training mix from news text to verified STEM/math data (ArmSTEM) recovers 18.3 Belebele points over the news-only run at the same high learning rate, and combined with a lower learning rate (3e-5) flips the outcome entirely, ending above the unadapted base model.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: A small, specific change in data composition (adding verified reasoning-heavy data) is what converts a failing language-adaptation recipe into a successful one — a transferable recipe for other low-resource-language efforts.

insights.claim: A 20% English replay ratio, the standard anti-forgetting technique, was present in every training run tested and did not by itself prevent catastrophic forgetting.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Challenges a widely assumed best practice in continual pretraining; suggests teams relying solely on generic replay ratios to prevent forgetting may be under-protected.
insights.quote:
The 20% English replay, the textbook
anti-forgetting lever, was present in every run and did not prevent
forgetting on its own.

insights.claim: The same forgetting pattern reproduces on a model the authors did not train: evaluating HyGPT-10b against its own Gemma-2-9B base on the same suite shows fluency improved (MultiBLiMP 0.971 to 0.996) while comprehension collapsed (Belebele 0.660 to 0.489) and the mean score fell (0.48 to 0.44).
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Cross-validates catastrophic forgetting as a systemic risk in language-adaptation fine-tuning generally, not an artifact specific to the authors' own pipeline — a warning flag for evaluating any vendor's 'language-adapted' LLM claims.

insights.claim: Token repetition is not what drives the recovery: a control run using the full 373K-item ArmSTEM corpus (about 1.3 passes) instead of the released 110K-item subset (7-9 passes) matches the released model on likelihood tasks, though the full-corpus run further lifts exam math score (1.75 to 2.75 points) and shifts the math-to-science data ratio.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Suggests data diversity/composition, not sheer repetition count, is the binding factor for downstream task performance — relevant for anyone tuning data-mixture ratios on a budget.

themes.theme: Transfer to generation without instruction tuning

insights.claim: arm-gemma-e4b, a base (non-instruction-tuned) model, outperforms the instruction-tuned ArmenianGPT-1.0-3B on the mean of 14 accuracy-style generative Armenian benchmark tasks (0.62 vs 0.57), because QA-shaped pretraining data taught it the required output format without dedicated instruction tuning.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Suggests that well-chosen pretraining data (QA-format-shaped) can substitute for costly instruction-tuning on format compliance, a cheaper path to usable low-resource-language models.

insights.claim: ArmenianGPT-1.0-3B still leads specifically on MMLU-Pro-Hy (0.281 vs 0.251 for arm-gemma-e4b), showing the new model's advantage is not universal across all task types.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: A caveat against over-generalizing the headline win; task-specific due diligence still matters when choosing a model for a specific Armenian-language application.

insights.claim: Part-of-speech tagging accuracy regresses under every single continued-pretraining run tested (0.18 down to 0.01), an unresolved capability loss regardless of data mixture or learning rate.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Flags a specific, consistent weakness that persists across all recipe variants tried — a known gap for anyone deploying this model line on syntax-sensitive tasks.

themes.theme: Benchmark contamination in public web crawls

insights.claim: Scanning Armenian-language slices of major public crawl datasets for benchmark contamination found ArmWeb's pre-release pool at 3.3% contaminated documents (removed before release) versus 7.9% for CulturaX-hy, 10.9% for HPLT-v2-hy, and 17.4% for FineWeb-2-hy.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Widely used multilingual pretraining corpora carry materially higher benchmark contamination for a lower-resource language than a purpose-built, decontaminated corpus — a red flag for trusting eval scores of models trained on generic multilingual crawls in low-resource languages.

insights.claim: Contamination overlap concentrates heavily in perplexity-style held-out test sets (themselves scraped from the web, e.g. FLORES, hyWiki), and FineWeb-2's own Armenian training split overlaps its own test split, while hand-built multiple-choice knowledge benchmarks show contamination at or below 0.06% for every corpus checked.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Perplexity-based leaderboard comparisons for Armenian (and plausibly other low-resource languages) are likely inflated and less trustworthy than knowledge-benchmark comparisons — investors evaluating LLM benchmark claims should weight eval methodology accordingly.

insights.claim: ArmWeb combined with CulturaX outperforms every individual corpus alone on held-out news perplexity at 410M-parameter scale, and the lead widens further at 1.3B parameters, indicating the new corpus is complementary to (not redundant with) existing crawls.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Suggests the best practical strategy is combining the new curated corpus with existing crawls rather than replacing them outright.

insights.claim: A scaling ladder of ablations from 70M to 1B parameters follows a clean power law that predicts a held-out 1.3B-parameter model's performance to within 0.47%, validating that conclusions from small-scale ablations transfer reliably to larger models.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: A cheap methodology (small-scale scaling-law extrapolation) for validating data/recipe decisions before committing to expensive large-model training runs — reusable beyond this project.

insights.claim: The ArmSTEM translation pipeline protects numbers and LaTeX with placeholder tokens, runs two feedback repair rounds with escalation to a stronger model on failure, applies a language-ID gate, and requires 'blind re-solving' where an independent model must reproduce the exact gold answer from the translated Armenian problem as the correctness check.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: A reusable, rigorous quality-assurance framework for machine-translating quantitative training data into other languages, applicable beyond Armenian.

insights.claim: After the repair process, 96.6% of translated ArmSTEM items survive verification (range 91.5-99.1% by source), and an independent human evaluation by two native speakers rated 299 of 300 sampled problems valid with perfect inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa = 1.0).
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Unusually rigorous, independently-audited QA for a machine-translated training dataset gives confidence the released data is trustworthy for downstream use, rare in most open translated corpora.

insights.claim: 10.9% of math items and 27.6% of science items in ArmSTEM are flagged as 'solver_limited' (unverifiable even when re-solved in the original English) rather than mistranslated, meaning a meaningful fraction of the dataset carries an explicit unverified-quality caveat.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Users reusing ArmSTEM should filter or weight the solver_limited subset differently, since it lacks the same verification guarantee as the rest of the corpus.

insights.claim: The authors explicitly frame the recipe as language-agnostic and reusable, stating that little in the pipeline is Armenian-specific beyond a language-ID label and a text-normalization table, positioning it as a template for adapting LLMs to any language with news archives.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Relevant to any team or investor targeting low-resource-language LLM deployment: this open recipe could be adapted directly rather than requiring de novo methodology development.
insights.quote:
if your language has news archives and needs
knowledge data, the recipe is yours to reuse.

insights.claim: The team plans a harder competition-math tranche of ArmSTEM and an instruction-tuned variant of arm-gemma-e4b to target the format-sensitive half of the ArmBench benchmark where current base-style models underperform.
insights.speaker: Erik Arakelyan
insights.so_what: Signals a near-term roadmap milestone (instruction-tuned release) worth tracking for anyone following open Armenian-language model progress.
